newsitem.title: SPAIN: Fury at communist threat to Spain constitution.
newsitem.headline: Fury at communist threat to Spain constitution.

text.p: Spanish politicians reacted with outrage on Monday to Communist Party suggestions that the country should scrap its 1978 constitution and monarchy and return to a pre-Civil War federal republic.

"It's the most worrying thing that has been uttered in Spain in recent years," Manuel Fraga, president of the northwestern region of Galicia and former leader of the conservative party which now rules in Madrid, told reporters on Monday.
"It's senseless and I hope it will be recognised as such and corrected," Fraga declared.

The outcry started after Communist Party (PCE) chief Julio Anguita told a party meeting at the weekend the PCE felt no obligation to honour a multi-party pact to defend Spain's cherished post-dictatorship constitution if the other parties were going to undermine its standards.
He said the government should be based on the republican government in place before and during the 1936-39 Civil War, with no monarchy and with more regional independence.

Angel Acebes, general coordinator for the ruling Popular Party (PP), rounded on Anguita on Monday. "It's a serious mistake," he said. He's raising a debate that doesn't exist in Spanish society, not even on the left, and one that is far from majority sentiment."
The PCE is the majority partner of the United Left (IU) coalition, which won 11 percent of the vote in general elections in March. It holds 21 of parliament's 350 seats.

Public support for the monarchy and King Juan Carlos, who played a key role in Spain's transition to democracy after nearly 40 years of dictatorship under General Francisco Franco, borders on the fanatic and Anguita's position was questioned even by other IU factions.
"He's talking about another world," said Cristina Almeida, a leading member of the New Left. "To go ahead with this discourse is to isolate us in the context of what people care about."

A cartoon in the daily El Mundo pointed to strong leftist support for the monarchy, with a relaxed looking Juan Carlos saying "It's logical that Anguita is a republican, but it's strange there are so many red (communist) monarchists."

Anguita's outburst late on Saturday climaxed two weeks of harsh attacks on the government for defying court requests to declassify a batch of secret files on a 1980s "dirty war" on Basque separatist guerrillas.
The files allegedly document the government's involvement in the 1983-87 campaign that killed 27 people.
The PCE contends the PP government, like the Socialists before it, breached constitutional principles by refusing to hand them over.
On Monday, the communist leader held a news conference to defend his "democratic right" to criticise the head of state and any other Spanish institution.
"(The king) is not immune to criticism," he said. "This is a constitutional democracy, not a theocracy, and the people are sovereign, not the monarch."

Anguita said King Juan Carlos had gone beyond constitutional bounds by speaking in support of Spain's full integration in NATO and commitment to the European Union, issues which Anguita said divide the population.
If the king were going to intervene, it should be to help ensure the courts functioned properly and fairly, he said.
"With the issue of NATO, the best thing the king could have done was to shut up. And with Maastricht, shut up.
"If he can't keep quiet about these issues, at least he could lend a hand to justice," Anguita said.
